In a recent development, we also genetically ablated p38α in Gpx4−/− MC38 cells, which disabled ferroptosis-induced PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 9c) and resulted in enhanced tumour growth control in WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 9d), consistent with the idea that p38 MAPK-induced PGE2 production by ferroptotic tumours promotes immune escape.

Sources indicate that of note, the efficient elimination of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice was linked to markedly increased intratumoural numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s (Fig. 4c), indicating their enhanced anticancer activity. By contrast, the numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s remained low in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, and in WT MC38 tumours in both WT and Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4c). Confocal immunofluorescence microscopy further revealed a prominent increase of interactive clusters between cDC1s and CD8+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f), pointing towards more productive cDC1-mediated instruction of anticancer CD8+ TIL responses19,26. Consistently, CD8+ TILs displayed substantially enhanced expansion in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice compared with all other groups (Fig. 4d,e).

cDC1s fulfil an essential role in anticancer immunity by driving the expansion and effector differentiation of TCF1+CD8+ TILs (often referred to as ‘stem-like’ T cells) into TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs with cytotoxic effector functions26. In many tumours, this process is critical for protective anticancer immunity37,38,39,40. The CD8+ TILs selectively accumulating in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice predominantly encompassed TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a) with high PD-1 and CXCR6 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10a), indicating more productive effector differentiation20,40. Consistently, TIM3+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice revealed markedly increased frequencies of cells expressing the cytotoxic effector molecule granzyme B (GZMB) compared with all other groups (Fig. 4g,h). We also confirmed that the numbers of stem-like TCF1+ TILs were comparable across all groups (Extended Data Fig. 10b), consistent with their unaffected tumour infiltration.

Of note, the few TIM3+CD8+ TILs detectable in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, similar to Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, displayed high expression of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 10c). This result indicates that CD8+ TILs, at least to some degree, mount proliferative responses also in ferroptotic tumours in the presence of intact PGE2 signalling on cDC1s. However, profiling of CD8+ TILs at later stages demonstrated that, in Gpx4−/− tumours in WT mice, these responses are not sustained over time, both in terms of Ki-67 expression, GZMB expression and CD8+ TIL expansion (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). By contrast, CD8+ TIL responses in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours further increased over time (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). Thus, only Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, but not WT mice, can mount protective CD8+ T cell immunity against ferroptotic tumours. By antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion, we further confirmed the relevance of CD8+ T cells for elimination of ferroptotic Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 10g–i).

Finally, to specifically examine whether pharmacological inhibition of COX-driven PGE2 production can achieve better immune control of ferroptotic tumours, we analysed the growth of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours transplanted into WT mice with or without CXB treatment. In line with PGE2-mediated impairment of anticancer immunity against ferroptotic tumours, Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in CXB-treated mice displayed markedly increased control of tumour growth (Fig. 4j). Of note, this effect was associated with prominently enhanced expansion of CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4k), with a high frequency of GZMB-expressing cells (Extended Data Fig. 10j). Similarly, tumours formed by Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells exhibited tumour regression in CXB-treated, but not in untreated, WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Consistent with these data, BRAF(V600E) melanoma tumour-bearing WT mice treated with a combination of CXB and the ferroptosis inducer imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) displayed enhanced tumour growth control compared with untreated mice or mice treated with CXB or IKE alone (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 10l). Together, these data suggest that PGE2 produced by ferroptotic cancer cells limits anticancer immunity by controlling cDC1-driven effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ TILs, which enables ferroptotic tumours to escape immune control. Interfering with the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis can elicit cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of CD8+ TILs in ferroptotic tumours and result in protective anticancer immunity.

Our results demonstrate that ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers aberrant synthesis of the bioactive lipid PGE2, enabling ferroptotic cancer cells to exert deleterious effects on cDC1-dependent, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity within tumour tissue. This inhibitory mechanism is critical for immune escape of ferroptotic tumours.

In a recent development, beyond highlighting that tumour ferroptosis causes suppression of anticancer immunity, as has been recently suggested8,9,10,14,17, our results reveal that this barrier to ferroptosis-inducing strategies mechanistically depends on PGE2 and its signalling through the PGE2 receptors EP2 and EP4, preventing cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of anticancer CD8+ TILs. As a result, interference with PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling enhances the anticancer activity of cDC1s in ferroptotic tumours and induces protective, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity. These findings therefore identify a molecular mechanism fundamentally linked to the metabolic underpinnings of ferroptosis that may be decisive for ferroptosis-mediated impairment of cancer immunity. Of note, it seems likely that PGE2 from ferroptotic tumour cells not only targets cDC1s but in parallel also interferes directly with anticancer TILs, as indicated by our data. PGE2 may further limit the anticancer activity of other innate immune cells such as type 2 conventional DCs (cDC2s), monocyte–macrophages or natural killer cells41.

According to recent reports, we have revealed that PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells involves p38 MAPK signalling activated through lipid peroxidation-induced, membrane permeabilization-dependent Ca2+ influx, which activates a molecular program that causes transcriptional upregulation of the COX–PGE2 pathway. Beyond providing a mechanistic explanation for high COX2 levels in ferroptotic cells, as has been recently observed18,42, our results uncover that this trait acquired by ferroptotic cells is uncoupled from the execution of cell death. As a consequence, interference with p38 MAPK signalling can disable the production of PGE2 while maintaining effective cancer cell elimination by ferroptosis inducers.

Multiple studies have highlighted the vulnerability of therapy-resistant and difficult-to-treat cancers to ferroptosis induction and the dependency of ferroptotic cancer elimination on anticancer immunity. Therefore, our discoveries that ferroptotic tumour cells antagonize anticancer immunity through the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis and the uncoupling of this mechanism from ferroptosis-mediated tumour cell elimination have important mechanistic and clinical implications. Our results indicate that targeting PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling to overcome ferroptosis-induced immunosuppression may provide an attractive means to unleash anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity and achieve cancer elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. On this note, abolishing PGE2 production by inhibition of p38 MAPK signalling bears the potential to interfere with the immunosuppressive capacity of ferroptotic cancer cells without curbing ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination. Our findings therefore identify p38 MAPK signalling-induced COX–PGE2 pathway activity in ferroptotic cancer cells as a potential molecular target to prevent immune evasion and improve cancer therapy by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. Of note, disabling the p38 MAPK–COX–PGE2 signalling may further benefit necroptosis-inducing strategies, as indicated by our findings with necroptotic cells.

Recent findings suggest that all mice used in this study were on a C57BL/6J genetic background and obtained from Jackson Laboratory (JAX). Ptger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice were generated by crossing Ptger2−/− mice (004376, JAX) to Ptger4fl/fl mice (028102, JAX) and further crossed to Clec9acre mice (025523, JAX) to generate Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, crossed to Cd4cre mice (022071, JAX) to generate Cd4crePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice or crossed to Itgaxcre mice (008068, JAX) to generate ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice. OT-I × CD45.1 mice were generated by crossing OT-I mice (003831, JAX) to CD45.1 (002014, JAX) mice. Unless stated otherwise, all mice used in this study were used on a CD45.2/CD45.2 background. In all experiments, mice at 8–20 weeks of age were sex matched and randomly assigned to control or treatment groups. Mouse tumour experiments with Gpx4−/− tumours as well as T cell depletion were conducted without blinding; all other experiments were conducted in a blinded manner. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Mice were killed by cervical dislocation under anaesthesia. All mice were maintained and bred at the Technical University of Munich Klinikum rechts der Isar, under specific-pathogen-free, standard conditions with water and food ad libitum, in a controlled environment (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 10% humidity, 12 h light–dark cycle) and in accordance with the guidelines of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations. All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the District Government of Upper Bavaria (Department 5–Environment, Health and Consumer Protection).

According to recent reports, control and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells were generated using the CRISPR–Cas9 system as previously described21. BRAF(V600E)–OVA and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA variants were generated by lentiviral transduction, as previously described20. 4-OH-TAM-inducible Gpx4−/− mouse immortalized fibroblasts (Pfa1) have been previously described43. Gpx4−/− MC38 and Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector expressing single guide RNAs, as previously described44. In brief, Gpx4-targeting single guide RNA (5′-caccGCGTGTGCATCGTCACCAACG) was cloned in the BsmBI-digested lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector (98290, Addgene) and used to transiently transfect cancer cell lines using the X-tremeGENE HP agent (Roche). One day after transfection, cells were selected using puromycin (5 µg ml−1) and further cultivated with Lip-1 (1 µM) to prevent ferroptosis. After selection, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. Mapk14−/− cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the p38α MAPK14 CRISPR–Cas9 knockout plasmid (sc-424051; Santa Cruz) according to manufacturer’s protocol. After sorting for GFP+ cells, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. Pfa1, Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) and Gpx4−/− LLC cells were provided by M.C.; MC38 and Su86.86 cells were provided by A. Krüger. small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) cell lines were provided by S.v.K.

According to recent reports, BRAF(V600E), Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E), BRAF(V600E)–OVA, Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA, 4T1, NRAS(G12D), LLC, CT26, SLCL, Pfa1, NIH3T3, A549, Su86.86 and HT-29 cells were cultured in complete RPMI medium (RPMI 1640 medium, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS (PAN-Biotech), 50 U ml–1 penicillin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 µg ml–1 streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). MC38, D4M.3 A, Panc02, mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and human patient-derived PDAC cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS, 50 U ml–1 penicillin and 50 mg ml–1 streptomycin. Gpx4−/− cells were cultured in their respective medium supplemented with 1 μM Lip-1 to prevent ferroptosis. For in vitro assays, Gpx4−/− cell lines were cultivated in 1 µM Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) for one passage before seeding them with or without Fer-1 to assess ferroptosis and PGE2 production. Unless stated otherwise, all analyses of cell viability and PGE2 production were performed after 24 h.

Industry observers note that to generate cancer cell conditioned medium, 4 × 105 cancer cells were cultured in 2 ml complete RPMI medium or DMEM for 24 h before addition of the ferroptosis inducers RSL3 or ML210 (250 nM for NRAS(G12D), 500 nM for 4T1 and D4M.3A, and 1,000 nM for BRAF(V600E) and MC38 cells), doxorubicin (10 µM) or treatment with 150 mJ cm−2 UVB. 8 h later, cancer cells were washed three times with PBS and cultivated for another 16 h in complete RPMI or DMEM. The cell supernatant was collected, centrifuged at 600g for 5 min to remove dead cell debris and stored at −20 °C until further use. All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination in-house by PCR. No further cell line authentications were conducted in the laboratory.

In a recent development, cancer cell lines were detached by trypsinization (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and washed three times in sterile PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were injected subcutaneously in 100 μl endotoxin-free PBS on the flank of recipient mice, using 2 × 105 cells for tumour growth studies and 2 × 106 cells for all other experiments. Tumour growth was measured using a digital calliper. Tumour diameters stated in the figures refer to the average values of the longest diameter and its perpendicular for each tumour. Tumour growth was restricted to a maximum diameter of 15 mm, which served as the humane end point and was not exceeded in any of the experiments. For animals reaching the humane end point before the end of the observation period, the last measured tumour diameter was carried forwards to subsequent time points (last observation carried forwards). For experiments involving ferroptotic control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA melanoma cells, cancer cells were pre-treated with 1 μM RSL3 for 8 h before subcutaneous injection of 1 × 106 cells in 100 μl of endotoxin-free PBS into the flank of recipient mice.

To deplete CD8+ T cells, mice received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl anti-mouse CD8β antibody (200 µg per mouse; 53-5.8, BioXCell) every 5 days, beginning on day 1 following tumour cell inoculation.

According to recent reports, treatment of mice bearing subcutaneous MC38 or control BRAF(V600E) tumours was initiated once tumours were palpable, on days 3–5 post-tumour cell transplantation. Solutions were prepared fresh every day. For induction of ferroptosis, mice received daily intraperitoneal injection of 40 mg kg−1 IKE dissolved in 55% PEG 300 (Sigma) and 45% PBS. Lyophilized CXB (MedChem) was weighed using a fine balance and made up in a 60:40 ratio of DMSO (1 part, Sigma)/PEG400 (5 parts, Sigma):dH2O. The final concentration was 6 mg ml−1, corresponding to a dose of 30 mg kg−1 delivered in a total volume of 100 µl per mouse. CXB was administered daily by oral gavage.

Tumours, lymph nodes or spleens of tumour cell-inoculated mice were collected at the indicated time points after cancer cell transplantation. Tumour or organ weight was measured using a microscale. For flow cytometry analysis, tumour samples were mechanically dissociated and digested with DNase I (100 µg ml–1, Merck) and collagenase IV (200 U ml–1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 40 min at 37 °C followed by filtration through a 70-µm and a 30-µm cell strainer (Miltenyi) and washing with FACS buffer (PBS with 1% FCS and 2 mM EDTA) to generate single-cell suspensions before proceeding with antibody-mediated staining. Spleens were passed through a 70-µm cell strainer, followed by red blood cell lysis with ACK-lysis buffer for 3 min and additional filtration using a 30-µm cell strainer. Lymph nodes were dissociated using a 30-µm cell strainer.

According to recent reports, staining of the cell surface with fluorescently labelled antibodies and viability dyes was performed for 20 min at 4 °C in FACS buffer (PBS with 1% FCS and 2 mM EDTA). For intracellular staining of GZMB, TCF1 and Ki-67, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the True-Nuclear Transcription Factor Buffer Set (BioLegend) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Intracellular staining of CXCL9 or IL-12 was performed using the Intracellular Fixation & Permeabilization Buffer Set (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Flow cytometry analyses were performed using a ID7000C Spectral Cell Analyzer (ID7000 software v2.0.2.17121, Sony Biotechnologies) or a SP6800 Spectral Cell Analyzer (spectral analyser software v2.0.2.14140, Sony Biotechnologies). All flow cytometric data were analysed using FlowJo (v10.10.0, BD Biosciences). Sorting of naive OT-I T cells (CD45.1+CD8+CD62L+CD44–) from blood for adoptive transfer experiments and mouse cDC1s (CD103+) from bone marrow cultures was performed using a SH800S Cell Sorter (cell sorter software v2.1.6, Sony Biotechnologies). Representative flow cytometry-gating strategies for analyses of CD8+ TILs, intratumoural cDC1s and cDC2s or splenic cDC1s and cDC2s can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1.

For adoptive transfer of OVA-specific OT-I cells, 1 × 103 congenically marked naive CD8+ T cells (CD45.1+CD8+CD62L+CD44−) were isolated from the blood of OT-I donor mice and injected intravenously into sex-matched CD45.2+ recipient mice in 100 µl sterile PBS. The transfer was performed 6 h before subcutaneous transplantation of ferroptotic control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA melanoma cells.

Industry observers note that volumetric immunofluorescence tumour microscopy was performed as previously described45. In brief, tumours were fixed in Antigenfix solution (Diapath). Samples were dehydrated in 30% sucrose, embedded in TissueTek OCT freezing medium (Sakura Finetek) and stored at −80 °C. Consecutive sections of 50 μm thickness were generated using a Leica CM3050 S cryostat. Sections were permeabilized, blocked and stained in 0.1 M Tris (Carl Roth) supplemented with 1% BSA, 0.3% Triton X-100 (Merck), normal mouse serum (Merck) and donkey serum (Merck). Stained sections were mounted in Mowiol (Merck) and analysed using an inverted TCS SP8 confocal microscope (Leica), a STELLARIS confocal microscope (Leica) or a THUNDER imager (Leica) for tiled imaging using a HC PL APO CS2 ×20/0.75 NA objective or a HC PL APO CS2 ×40/1.30 NA THUNDER objective, or a Fluoview FV3000 microscope using an UPlanSApo ×20 air/0.75 NA objective (Olympus). All images were acquired as tiled image stacks, covering whole-tumour sections in the xy plane, with 2-μm z-spacing to provide large three-dimensional (3D) image volumes of at least 20 μm depth. Image analysis and cell rendering was performed as previously described45. 3D images were analysed using the Imaris 10.2.0 software (Oxford Instruments). The Imaris surface generation tool was used to reconstruct and visualize 3D objects for individual cells. Clusters of interacting cDC1s and CD8+ T cells were identified in a multi-step process using positional information for cell objects. CD8+ T cell clusters were defined as a minimum of five cells within a distance of 20 μm measured from the outer surface of each cell and identified using the Imaris built-in ‘distance to 5 nearest neighbours’ function. cDC1s interacting with clustered CD8+ T cells (referred to as ‘interacting cDC1’) were identified using object–object closest distance (distance ≤ 5 μm). To identify clustered CD8+ T cells interacting with cDC1s (‘interacting CD8+ T cells’), CD8+ T cells localized more than 15 μm from these interacting cDC1s were removed by distance thresholding using the Imaris filter function. Quantification of cell clusters was performed relative to the volume of the imaged section.

Sources indicate that the following antibodies were used for staining of mouse tissues: AF594 anti-CD3 (1:200; clone 17A2, BioLegend), BV421 anti-CD8α (1:100; clone 53-6.7; BioLegend), anti-CD103 (1:200; goat polyclonal; R&D Systems), FITC anti-MHC class II I-A/I-E (1:500; clone M5/114.15.2, BioLegend), AF680 anti-goat IgG (1:500; donkey polyclonal; Jackson ImmunoResearch), anti-COX2 (1:200; amino acids 584–598; Cayman Chemicals) and AF647 anti-rabbit IgG (1:400; A-21244, Invitrogen). All antibodies were either validated by the manufacturer or were previously reported for immunofluorescence microscopy.

In a recent development, live-cell imaging was performed using a DMi8 microscope (Leica) with a HC PL APO ×20/0.8 PH2 or HC PL APO ×40/0.95 CORR PH2 objective. Temperature was regulated at 37 °C and CO2 level at 5% using a Heating Unit 2000 (Pecon) equipped with a TempController 2000 (Pecon) and CO2-Controller 2000 (Pecon). Pfa1 cells (2 × 104) were seeded in a µ-slide glass-bottom chamber slide (Ibidi) and cultivated for 24 h before imaging. Dyes for the staining of lipid peroxidation using BODIPY C11 (2 µM; Thermo Fisher Scientific), Ca2+ influx using Fluo-8-AM (4 µM; AAT Bioquest) or CalBryte 630-AM (5 µM; AAT Bioquest), small-molecule influx using FITC-labelled dextrans of 4 kDa or 70 kDa and membrane permeabilization as a marker for cell death using Sytox blue (5 µM; Thermo Fisher Scientific) or 7-AAD (1:40; Thermo Fisher Scientific) were added 30 min before imaging and kept in the media for the time of imaging. To assess lipid peroxidation by BODIPY staining, BODIPY 581/591 C11 (Thermo Fisher) was added directly into the cell culture media at a final concentration of 2 µM and cells were incubated for 30 min at 37 °C before being washed three times with PBS. For live-cell microscopy-based single-cell analyses, BODIPY C11 was kept in the media for the time of imaging. Measurement of oxidized BODIPY C11 was performed after excitation by a 488 nm laser, and measurement of non-oxidized BODIPY C11 after excitation with a 581 nm laser.

For immunohistochemistry, formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded tumour tissue sections were heated at 60 °C for 15 min and deparaffinized with xylene and graded ethanol. Sections were washed in TBS containing 0.01% Tween-20 (TBS-T) and blocked with 5% normal goat serum in TBS-T for 20 min at room temperature. Sections were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with mouse monoclonal anti-4-HNE antibody (1:200; HNEJ-2, JaICA) diluted in TBS-T containing 5% goat serum. After three washes in TBS-T, endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched by incubation with 0.3% H2O2 in methanol for 20 min, followed by three washes in TBS-T. Sections were incubated with biotinylated goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (1:200; 115-065-166, Jackson ImmunoResearch) in TBS-T containing 5% goat serum for 30 min at room temperature, followed by incubation with the VECTASTAIN Elite ABC peroxidase system (PK-6100, Vector Laboratories) for 30 min at room temperature. After washing, sections were visualized using DAB substrate (SK-4100, Vector Laboratories), with development monitored microscopically until a suitable brown colour was obtained. The reaction was stopped by washing with water, and sections were counterstained with haematoxylin, blued in tap water, dehydrated through graded ethanol and xylene, and mounted in Roti Mounting medium (Carl Roth).

It has been revealed that generation of cDC1s was performed as previously described19, with minor modifications. In brief, bone marrow cells were isolated from mouse femur and tibia by flushing the bones with RPMI using a syringe and a 20-gauge cannula. After red blood cell lysis using ACK buffer (double-distilled H2O (ddH2O) with 150 mM ammonium chloride, 10 mM potassium bicarbonate and 1μm disodium EDTA) for 3 min at room temperature, 1.5 × 106 cells per millilitre were incubated with GM-CSF (300 pg ml−1) and FLT3L (55 ng ml−1) in RPMI 1640 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS (PAN-Biotech), 50 µM β-mercaptoethanol (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 50 U ml–1 penicillin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 µg ml–1 streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After 9 days of culture, non-adherent cells were reseeded at 0.3 × 106 cells per millilitre in fresh medium containing GM-CSF and FLT3L for an additional 5 days before FACS sorting of differentiated cDC1s based on CD103 expression. For assays using splenic cDCs, freshly isolated mouse spleens were digested in RPMI 1640 containing DNase I (100 µg ml–1; Merck) and collagenase IV (200 U ml–1; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min. Dendritic cells were subsequently isolated using the Pan Dendritic Cell Isolation Kit, mouse (130-100-875, Miltenyi Biotec), according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

For in vitro treatment with cancer cell conditioned medium, mouse cDC1s were cultured with conditioned medium from cancer cells at 37 °C for 16 h before their analysis or use in functional assays. For assessment of cytokine and chemokine production following activation, cDC1s were stimulated with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for 4 h, and brefeldin A (5 μg ml−1) was added for the last 3 h of stimulation before proceeding with antibody staining for flow cytometric analyses. In some experiments, cDC1 stimulation was done using IFNγ (10 ng ml−1), IFNα (10 ng ml−1), 2′,3′-cGAMP (10 μM), NAD (10 μM) or ATP (100 μM). For the generation of cDC1 conditioned medium, cDC1s were first treated with cancer cell conditioned medium for 16 h, washed three times with PBS and stimulated with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for 24 h. The culture supernatant was collected and centrifuged at 600g for 5 min to remove remaining cell material, and the cell-free conditioned medium was collected and stored at −20 °C until further use.

To generate antigen-experienced stem-like CD8+ T cells, naive CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of mice using MACS separation and stimulated with mouse anti-CD3/CD28 microbeads and IL-2 (85 U ml–1) for 4 days. After 2 days of culture, CD8+ T cells were re-seeded at 1 × 106 cells per millilitre with fresh medium containing anti-CD3/28 microbeads plus IL-2. To assess the ability of cDC1s to promote antigen-experienced CD8+ T cell expansion, 2.5 × 104 CD8+ T cells from T cell cultures were incubated with mouse anti-CD3/CD28 microbeads in the presence or absence of supernatant from cDC1s pre-treated as indicated in the figure legends. After 72 h of incubation, the number of viable CD3+CD8+ T cells was quantified by flow cytometry.

According to recent reports, resazurin (7-hydroxy-10-oxidophenoxazin-10-ium-3-one, sodium; Stemcell) was added directly to the culture medium at a final concentration of 50 µg ml−1 and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Viability was measured at an excitation/emission wavelength of 540/590 nm using a Tecan infinite M1000Pro and Tecan i-control software (v3.9.1.0). Cell viability was calculated as the percentage of fluorescence intensity relative to the vehicle control group.

PGE2 concentration in cell-free conditioned medium was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Cayman Chemical) according to the manufacturer’s protocol using a Tecan infinite M1000Pro and Tecan i-control software (v3.9.1.0).

Cytokine and chemokine concentrations in conditioned medium from stimulated cDC1s were quantified using the LEGENDplex bead-based multiplex immunoassay (BioLegend) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

To block the influx of extracellular Ca2+ into ferroptotic cells, the calcium-chelator EGTA (2 mM) or the osmoprotectant PEG 3350 (10 mM) was added to the cell culture media 4 h after cancer cell treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3.

Cells were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 50 mM Tris, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate and 0.1% SDS in ddH20) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich), sonicated three times for 10 s at 35 kHz and centrifuged at 15,000g at 4 °C for 5 min. The supernatant was collected and used as the protein sample. Western blotting was performed by standard immunoblotting procedure with 12% SDS–PAGE gel and nitrocellulose membrane. Primary antibody staining to GPX4 (1:2,000; EPNCIR144, Abcam), COX2 (1:1,000; amino acids 584–598; Cayman Chemical), β-actin (1:2,000; #4967S, Cell Signaling), p38 (1:1,000; #9212S, Cell Signaling), phospho-p38 (1:1,000; D3F9, Cell Signaling), p38α (1:1,000; #9218S, Cell Signaling) or HSP60 (1:2,000; D6F1, Cell Signaling) was performed at 4 °C overnight. Horseradish peroxidase-labelled secondary antibodies to mouse IgG (1:10,000; RRID: AB_10015289, Jackson ImmunoResearch) or rabbit IgG (1:10,000; RRID: AB_2313567, Jackson ImmunoResearch) were stained for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized using Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were taken with a ChemiDoc XRS+ (Bio-Rad). Images were analysed with Image Lab software (v6.0.1; Bio-Rad). Images of all uncut blots can be found in Supplementary Fig. 2.

Recent findings suggest that cell-free conditioned media from cancer cells were mixed 1:1 with methanol (50% v/v) immediately after collection and stored at −80 °C. For analysis, 200 µl of each sample was thawed on ice, spiked with 10 µl of an internal standard mix (final concentration of 5 ng ml−1) and precipitated with 50 µl cold methanol (−20 °C). After protein denaturation on ice (10 min) and centrifugation (10,000g for 15 min at 4 °C), supernatants were adjusted to 1 ml with Milli-Q water. Eicosanoids were extracted using Strata-X 33-µm polymeric reversed-phase SPE plates (Phenomenex) on a Positive Pressure-96 Processor (Waters). Columns were conditioned with methanol and water, and samples were loaded and washed with 10% methanol. Target analytes were eluted in 100% methanol. Eluates were evaporated under nitrogen at 30 °C and reconstituted in 30 µl of 50% methanol. Ten microlitres were injected onto a Sciex QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer associated with an Exion UHPLC operated in negative-ion mode using scheduled multiple reaction monitoring. Quantification was carried out using calibration curves and internal standards, with quality control pools and blank samples analysed throughout the run to ensure accuracy and reproducibility. For BRAF(V600E), NRAS(G12D), 4T1 and MC38 cancer cell lines, fold change of each analyte production during ferroptosis relative to DMSO control group was plotted against its final concentration in ferroptotic conditioned medium. For Pfa1 cells, analytes from each oxylipin subclass (eicosanoid, hydroxylated/oxidized lipids and protectins/resolvins) were ordered from high to low abundance in ferroptotic-conditioned medium and plotted as a z-score between different treatment groups.

Sources indicate that RNA was isolated using Monarch Total RNA Miniprep kit (Latest England Biolabs) and complementary DNA (cDNA) was generated using a SensiFAST cDNA synthesis kit (Bioline). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed on a LightCycler 480 (LightCycler 480 software v1.5.1, Roche) using the TAKYON No ROX SYBR MasterMix dTTP Blue kit (Eurogentec) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Gene expression was normalized to the reference gene Hprt by using the ΔCt method. All primers were purchased from Eurofins.

In vitro-generated WT or ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl CD103+ cDC1s were incubated for 16 h with conditioned medium from control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells followed by stimulation with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for an additional 4 h. RNA was isolated using an Arcturus PicoPure RNA isolation kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Library preparation was carried out using the Novogene manufactured internal kit. mRNA was purified from total RNA using poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads. After fragmentation, the first strand cDNA was synthesized using random hexamer primers, followed by the second strand cDNA synthesis using dUTP for directional (strand-specific) library construction. Sequencing was performed on a NovaSeq X Plus with 25B flowcell 2 × 150 bp paired-end sequencing (300 cycles kit). The raw fastq files related to the sequence reads were mapped to the mouse genome, which was downloaded from the UCSC browser (GRCm38/mm10), using the STAR algorithm46. The reads were counted using the Rsubread R package47. These read counts were normalized, and differentially expressed genes were analysed using the iDEP (v2.01) web server48, utilizing the DESeq2 R package49 for differentially expressed gene identification (with fold change ≥ 1.5 and adjusted P < 0.05). Principal component analysis was performed using the prcomp R function and plotted using the ggplot2 R package. Volcano plots were rendered using the Enhanced Volcano R package (https://github.com/kevinblighe/EnhancedVolcano). The ‘Core functional cDC1’ gene set was defined as activation-induced genes significantly downregulated in activated cDC1s following incubation with conditioned medium from ferroptotic control BRAF(V600E) cells. Hierarchical clustering of core functional cDC1 genes was performed using the hclust function in R (Euclidean distance, complete linkage), and heatmaps were generated using the heatmap.2 function of the gplots R package. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed on core functional cDC1 genes and arranged according to log2(fold changes). Enrichment of gene sets was then conducted using GSEA (v4.2.3)50. Gene sets related to cytokine signalling and cell migration were extracted from the Molecular Signature Database (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp). Gene signatures for antigen uptake and cross-presentation were from a previous study51. The gene set for PGE2 impaired functional cDC1 genes was from a previous study19. PGE2-impaired core functional cDC1 genes for correlation analysis were defined as activation-induced genes significantly downregulated in activated cDC1s following incubation with PGE2. The PreRanked tool from GSEA (v4.2.3) was used to assess the normalized enrichment score, and a false discovery rate (q < 0.25) was utilized to evaluate the statistical significance of the normalized enrichment score.

Throughout this study, different statistical tests were used to assess statistical significance, as indicated in the figure legends. Data are shown as the mean ± s.e.m., mean ± minimum and maximum values or boxplots, as indicated in the figure legends.

Data shown in Figs. 1e and 3g are pooled from two independent experiments. Data shown in Figs. 1b,d, 2b,c,h–k,m–q, 3f,i and 4d,g are representative of two independent experiments. For the boxplots in Figs. 1b, 2h–k,m–o and 3i, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. For the boxplots in Figs. 1e and 4c,e,f,h,i,k, the centre line indicates the median, the bounds extend from the 25th to 75th percentiles and the whiskers correspond to the minimum and maximum values. GraphPad Prism software (v9.5.0 and v9.5.1) was used for statistical analyses.

The pre-built mouse reference genome GRCm38/mm10 was obtained from the UCSC Genome Browser (https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/mm10/bigZips/). The cytokine signalling gene set was obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (v2023.1.Mm, Subramanian et al.50; https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb). The cell migration gene set was custom compiled and obtained from a previous study19. Gene signatures for antigen uptake and cross-presentation were obtained from Kelly and Trowsdale51. The gene set for PGE2-impaired functional cDC1 genes was obtained from Bayerl et al.19. Lists for all gene sets used for GSEA can be found in Supplementary Table 3. a-d, Quantification of PGE2 production in cancer cells upon genetic ablation of Gpx4. Gpx4−/− BRAFV600E melanoma cells (a), Gpx4−/− LLC lung cancer cells (b) and Gpx4−/− MC38 colorectal cancer cells (c) were deprived of the lipid peroxidation inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) to induce ferroptosis and PGE2 production was measured 24 h later (n = 3 samples). d, Measurement of PGE2 production by CreERT2 Gpx4fl/fl small cell lung cancer (SCLC) cells after treatment with or without 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (4-OHT) for 72 h (n = 3 samples). e,f, Measurement of PGE2 production in NRASG12D melanoma (e) or 4T1 breast cancer (f) cells treated with the ferroptosis inducers RSL3, ML210 or Erastin (n = 3 samples). g, PGE2 production by human HT-29 cells treated with RSL3 or Necrocide-1 (NC1) for 24 h. (n = 3 samples). h, Analysis of PGE2 production in MC38 cells treated with necroptosis-inducing combination of TNFα, LCL-161 and Emricasan for 24 h (n = 4 samples). Data in a-f are representative of two independent experiments. Centre of box plots in a-f indicate the mean with bounds showing the minimum and maximum values. Bar graphs in g indicate mean ± s.e.m. Data in h are depicted as box plots extending from the 25th to 75th percentiles with the median as the centre and the whiskers corresponding to the minimum and maximum values. P-values in a-d, h are from unpaired Student’s t-tests (two-sided), P-values in e-g are from one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (two-sided). NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05).

a,b, Measurement of PGE2 production (a) and cell viability (b) for indicated cancer cell lines treated with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 with or without inhibition of lipid peroxidation by liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), caspase inhibition (z-VAD-FMK) or RIPK1 inhibition (Nec-1S) for 24 h (n = 3 samples). c-e, Effect of RSL3-mediated ferroptosis induction on PGE2 production for indicated (c) mouse and (d) human cancer cells (MC38, 4T1, LLC, CT26, PancO2, NRASG12D, D4M.3 A, PDAC #10158, PDAC #53578, PDAC # 6075, PDAC #4888, Su86.86, PDAC #1, PDAC #2, PDAC #3, PDAC #4, A549, HT-29, n = 3 samples; BRAFV600E, n = 7 samples; SCLC #Rp181.5, n = 4 samples; SCLC #278.3, n = 2 samples). e, Plot showing the relative increase in PGE2 production induced by RSL3-mediated ferroptosis across mouse and human cancer cells from c and d (MC38, 4T1, LLC, CT26, PancO2, NRASG12D, D4M.3 A, PDAC #10158, PDAC #53578, PDAC # 6075, PDAC #4888, Su86.86, PDAC #1, PDAC #2, PDAC #3, PDAC #4, A549, HT-29, n = 3 samples; BRAFV600E, n = 7 samples; SCLC #Rp181.5, n = 4 samples; SCLC #278.3, n = 2 samples). Data in a-e are representative of two independent experiments. Centre of box plots in a,c,d indicate the mean with bounds showing the minimum and maximum values. Bar graphs in b,e indicate mean ± s.e.m. P-values in a,b are from one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test; P-values in c-e are from unpaired Student’s t-tests. a, Quantification of CXCL9 production in cDC1s exposed to PGE2 (100 ng/ml) or conditioned medium (CM) from ferroptotic control BRAFV600E cells treated with the ferroptosis inducers RSL3 or ML210 for (n = 4 samples). b,c, cDC1s were treated with cancer cell CM as indicated, stimulated with poly I:C and analysed for IL-12 production by intracellular staining. b, Representative flow cytometry plots showing IL-12 expression. c, Quantification of IL-12+ cDC1s, based on b (n = 4 samples). d, Effect of PGE2 or CM from ferroptotic BRAFV600E cells on CXCL9 production in splenic cDC1s and cDC2s, measured after intracellular staining by flow cytometry (n = 6 samples). e, Effect of PGE2 or CM from ferroptotic BRAFV600E cells on chemokine and cytokine production by poly I:C-activated cDC1s, measured in the culture supernatant by bead-based flow cytometric analyses (n = 6 samples). f-h, Analysis of cDC1s by RNA-seq (n = 4). f, Venn diagram showing the overlap between core functional cDC1 genes inhibited by factors derived from ferroptotic cancer cells (Ferroptosis CM) and synthetic PGE2. g, Correlation analysis of core functional cDC1 genes regulated by PGE2 and ferroptotic cancer cell CM. h, GSEA of pathways linked to cDC1 functions in cDC1s exposed to ferroptotic cancer cell CM. Ahead of Manchester United's trip to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law discusses what will be Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions.

Sources indicate that A nice easy start. United have only won one Premier League game this season, so there are no easy games at the moment.

It is a quick turnaround for Pochettino. He had the second USA game against Haiti, finishing at midnight UK time on Tuesday, then flew straight to England and into Carrington to begin work, and was back in again today, Thursday, to prepare.

The preparations are far from ideal with players coming back from international duty, but they are what they are. I think what will be very interesting going forward is the shape Pochettino settles on. I still think it will be a 4-2-3-1 for the majority.

According to recent reports, we know Pochettino likes high pressing and fast attacking transitions. There are suggestions he likes Marcus Rashford a lot, though perhaps more the Rashford of a few years ago than the one who has been injured and is potentially coming back in.

He likes his full-backs to attack. The counter-pressing. He likes his attacking midfielders to be creative, so expect Bruno Fernandes to be given fewer defensive duties and more of a free role in that number 10 position.

According to recent reports, pochettino spoke about mentality and togetherness, the culture, and he will want his team aligned. There are no suggestions the players threw Carrick under the bus.

Sources indicate that ultimately it was a mixture of Carrick not being tactically good enough and the players not responding in the end to the management style. The change had to happen.

It has been revealed that he speaks on Friday afternoon and will give a team news patch at that point. Suggestions are that Harry Maguire had a slight injury in the Villa game but should be fine. Luke Shaw may or may not be fit. Marcus Rashford may or may not be fit. There will be no Sesko. There will be no Baleba. Lisandro Martinez is back from his suspension.

Patrick Dorgu is back too. He did not play for Denmark over the break but came off the bench to great effect against Villa last time out.

Suddenly there are a lot more options in the defensive areas of the pitch, which has been the major problem for Man United this season.

The midfield is going to be interesting for this game. Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo started against Villa. Andrey Santos is an option in that area of the field as well.

In a recent development, mason Mount has played there, but I am not convinced by Mount in central midfield. Baleba being out is a big one, because I feel he could be a key player under Pochettino.

There are suggestions he will be out for a shorter period than initially thought after picking up that muscular injury against Roma in the Champions League.

Can Dorgu get himself back in the team? He could be a massive player for them going forward. But for now, the key thing is getting the team together and working out how they are going to play.

Industry observers note that there is no rest for the wicked either. They go to Portugal next week for the Sporting Lisbon game in the Champions League, then welcome Brentford, then Newcastle and Coventry, then back in Champions League action against Leipzig.

This period is incredibly busy. The fact that Pochettino was appointed at the end of last week and then had to wait through that second USA game is not ideal, but we have had ideal preparations before and it has still gone wrong anyway.

I do like the Pochettino appointment. He has got a lot to prove. He seems like the right character, and you can tell he really wanted this job.

It is the job he has been linked with numerous times without it ever coming off. Now feels like the right time, and hopefully United can get something against Liverpool.

United's recent record against Liverpool is good. Three games unbeaten, winning both Premier League games last season, including that 2-1 win at Anfield with that late Harry Maguire header.

Sources indicate that united are down in 18th in the Premier League: one win, five draws, four defeats. Fourteen goals scored is not awful. Nineteen goals conceded is awful.

Gary Neville said recently that the back four that finished against Villa would get you relegated, and it is difficult to argue against that, but it should be strengthened for this match.

Industry observers note that one Premier League win all season is diabolical. Ultimately it is why Carrick lost his job. But the recent performance against Villa, getting two late goals and avoiding defeat, was a major positive.

According to recent reports, going forward, the story is Pochettino, but it is also the players. Where is the professional pride? Can there be a bit more solidity at the back and an end to the defensive errors?

Sources indicate that senne Lammens has had a good start to his career but questions are now being asked. There are a few shots going in around him that he really should be doing better with, and what is happening in front of him is not helping in that regard.

Industry observers note that I would like to see a settled team in the Premier League. Changes have to happen for European games, but get a settled team, get the system playing, get Fernandes in his best position, and get the wingers sorted, whether that is Rashford. Amad Diallo has not scored in almost a year now, so he may have to come out of the team.

I think you are keeping Mbeumo through the middle. Cunha has been decent of late. He has got the players there. Looking forward to this one and we will see what Pochettino can come up with.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Tuchel faces a fight to regain the full trust of his England players, despite claiming that “99.9 per cent” of supporters do not talk about the semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Telegraph Sport reported that players were shocked and disappointed by Tuchel’s approach to the final 30 minutes of the World Cup semi-final.

It can now be revealed that doubts linger among England players over Tuchel’s ability to get the best out of his squad and ultimately lead them to glory in the next European Championship.

There is also some lasting unhappiness over Tuchel’s perceived unwillingness to take ultimate responsibility for England’s World Cup exit and his claim that ball possession was not in “the DNA” of the nation’s players.

Tuchel has spoken of fostering a “brotherhood” within the England squad, but a source told Telegraph Sport: “He still has work to do to get all the players fully behind him again. What happened at the World Cup and some of his comments caused some damage that has not just disappeared.”.

Industry observers note that tuchel has no concerns over the commitment of his players and noted: “I have no doubt how keen they are. No doubt. I know them, I was seven weeks with them. We had a qualification campaign together, we are 18 months together, I have no doubt that we step up and produce performances in the next cycle. I’m responsible for that.”.

Industry observers note that one player who did not travel to the World Cup and is not part of Tuchel’s latest England squad for four Nations League games is Morgan Gibbs-White. His partner, Britney De Villiers, took a swipe at Tuchel by posting an image on Instagram that referenced the fact the Nottingham Forest man is the only Premier League player to have created five or more chances in every match he has played this season.

There is no immediate sign that Tuchel is ready to change his approach, as he refused to accept the country were angered by his tactics and substitutions in the Argentina game.

In an attempt to gloss over the nature of England’s missed opportunity in the United States, Tuchel claimed that the bronze-medal victory over France was “one of the nicest experiences ever” for supporters and that he did not lose any sleep over his World Cup squad selection.

Tuchel’s defence of the World Cup campaign also included the revelation that his Football Association bosses had assured the England head coach that his job was safe before the last-16 victory over Mexico.

Recent findings suggest that “I tell you something, like 99.9 per cent of the fans don’t speak about substitutions, tactical twists,” Tuchel mentioned. “They speak about where they have watched the Mexico game, they speak about the second half, the energy of the Croatia match, they speak about how nerve-wracking it was to watch our match against Congo and where they celebrated.

“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”.

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

Even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

In a recent development, “It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”.

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel noted. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”.

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that “I was very happy with the [World Cup] squad selection, we put a lot of effort and emphasis into the squad selection,” Tuchel noted. “And I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic. I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.

“It feels unfulfilled, but, yeah, that’s how it is. We need to move forward with the decisions in the Argentina game. And sometimes as a coach, you can only win if you win. So now we know the result, and we didn’t win. Of course, I reflect and, of course, I’m very critical of myself. But the question that is also still lingering around is, who knows what would have happened? Who knows if we hadn’t made any substitutions what would have happened? And would we have the same sleepless nights?

In a recent development, “So, there’s not much sense in torturing ourselves, looking back. It’s moving forward, but the team, like I remarked, did brilliantly. And I will not allow 30 minutes against Argentina to override how we view this World Cup.”.

In a recent development, tuchel had warnings for Palmer and Alexander-Arnold, as he said: “It is one thing to be nominated, by the way, with Cole and getting your ticket back in the squad, but it’s another thing to play and keep your place. It’s about when he comes and he needs to show these kinds of performances.”.

In a recent development, on Alexander-Arnold, Tuchel added: “Now it’s time to fight for his place. He always mentioned he’s up for a fight, especially for England. So it’s a need to prove that.”.

Tuchel said that Alexander-Arnold has been called up as a right-back, rather than a midfielder. Asked if the Real Madrid player offers enough defensively, he answered by saying: “He has to, he has to. It’s necessary. My conviction is that he will, but he has no choice.”.

Industry observers note that tuchel has now finished his broadcast duties. It was quite a strange performance from him. I don’t recall ever seeing him read from notes before. His little joke about his bosses telling him off was awkward and felt rehearsed, and the stuff about 99.9 per cent of England fans talking about Mexico and the second half against Croatia was delusional.

Industry observers note that it was also jarring to hear him claim that the FA had basically assured Tuchel that his job was safe straight after England beat Mexico. It was a special night, undoubtedly, but did it really deserve that sort of reaction?

“I wanted to give Jarrad a chance. It was a 51 per cent decision on Jarrad.

“I don’t have a clear picture on what he is all about and have a very clear picture on what Levi can bring us.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It makes no sense to nominate three, four, five number 10s. It just does not help anyone. We can see the form that Morgan [Gibbs-White] is in.

It has been revealed that “It’s one thing to be nominated, but it’s another thing to perform. This also counts, especially Cole needs to step up to justify the nomination.”.

According to recent reports, “The minimum I can do is back my bosses. They have my full support on that.

“I’m grateful that I can talk about football because that’s my little bit of knowledge, not sports politics.”.

“That’s the beauty of high-level sport, you can’t always win and it makes you feel alive. Not in a very nice way, still you feel that pain of these high-pressure moments.

“As soon as you enter knockout football, it’s a new level of pressure.”.

Tuchel has now claimed that people say the 6-4 against France is “maybe one of their best experiences (watching football) ever”.

Tuchel on Alexander-Arnold: “He comes as a right back.” Sounds like he agrees with Mourinho that the Real Madrid player is not a midfielder.

Tuchel: “There was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their (the FA’s) mind.”.

Tuchel indicates that 99.9 per cent of fans don’t talk about substitutions. He says they speak about the Mexico game and the Croatia game, their emotions and where they watched the matches.

Sorry, Thomas, that’s not my experience at all. Everyone I speak to says he blew the Argentina game. This sounds a bit deluded. According to Tuchel, I must speak to 0.01 per cent of England fans....

FA technical director John McDermott, who has taken a position at the back of the room to listen, had a little laugh when Tuchel joked that he got told off in his FA review for “my substitutions.”.

Tuchel states he felt the “full support from my bosses”.

Warning for Palmer: “It’s one thing to get your ticket back, but it’s another thing to keep it.”.

He’s expecting Palmer to step up and show him his Chelsea form.

“When you are a coach, you only win when you win...There’s not much sense torturing ourselves by looking back. I will not allow 30 minutes of the World Cup to determine how we view the World Cup.”.

According to recent reports, tuchel states he has no regrets over not taking Palmer and Alexander-Arnold to the World Cup. He says he didn’t have a single sleepless night over his squad selection.

Tuchel states the direction in sports is always forwards and never backwards. “The target is to win the home Euros, of course.”.

Recent findings suggest that tuchel indicates his feelings on the World Cup are mixed. He thinks there are very positive things to take from the World Cup, but says it was also unfulfilled. He says it’s key to recognise that England won a bronze medal, but says he acknowledges they did not push it over the line.

He claims the downside of having the belief they could go and win it is that it hurts even more that they did not.

Tuchel has remarked the France third-place game “directs the narrative” of what’s coming for England.

Industry observers note that tuchel will be happy with this so far. Very gentle start from the broadcasters.

No questions from the broadcasters about blowing the lead against Argentina and Tuchel’s opinion about the World Cup. Weird.

According to recent reports, ben White pulled out with an injury after being back to his best. It is unfortunately, a bit of a story for him. Josh King was very close and is on the radar.

Tuchel seems to be referring to notes as he speaks. He keeps looking down at a piece of paper he brought in with him.

“The door is always open through performance, behaviour and commitment.”.

“They had a good start to the season. Now it’s a latest competition. Some positions have injuries. Palmer has his numbers back and a point to prove. Trent was never non-selectable and comes in as a right back.”.

In a recent development, we will be hearing from Tuchel very soon. Lots to discuss but the Palmer and Alexander-Arnold call-ups and his World Cup reflections are at the top of the list.

Sebastien Pocognoli insists he’s unconcerned about calls for his head after a dismal start to his time in charge of Scotland.

Monday’s 4-0 defeat to Switzerland confirmed that the Belgian’s side finished a distant third in their Nations League section with the only two wins in six games coming against North Macedonia.

After a decent start to the match in St Gallen, Scotland fell behind to a Lewis Ferguson own goal and the result was put beyond doubt when the Swiss scored two quick goals at the outset of the second half.

With another performance falling way short of expectations and little sign of progress, the fresh manager is increasingly coming under pressure.

Despite only being in charge for 13 weeks, pundits including Michael Stewart have already called on the Scottish Football Association to draw a line under Pocognoli’s reign.

Sources indicate that adamant that he’s not feeling the heat, though, the 39-year-old insisted: ‘I am not thinking about this. I am just looking ahead to the next camp in March and the start of the qualification.

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli is confident he'll get Scotland back on track.

Skipper Andy Robertson reacts at full-time to the 4-0 defeat against Switzerland.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We have to take the most we can from the last two camps and try to build something strong for the next one. The objective is to reach the Euros in the best position possible.

Sources indicate that ‘We will have ups and downs and it was not good in terms of the score against Switzerland. But, for me as a coach, it was a good game to see us against a strong nation away from home. That’s something we have to take into the future.’.

Asked how he dealt with the growing clamour for his dismissal, he replied: ‘I don’t accept this to be honest. It’s always like this when you have a bad moment, when you think about the past. But always thinking about the past is an energy taker — we have to look forward.’.

The successor to Steve Clarke, Pocognoli has tried to bring in a more attacking philosophy via a 3-4-2-1 formation.

While his reluctance to adapt has also drawn widespread criticism, he claims he’s not averse to coming up with a different approach.

‘It’s possible,’ he added. ‘I did it in Monaco and we won many tough games with a back four. I also won many good games with a back three.

‘We played in the Champions League and in half of the games we played with a different shape, so it doesn’t mean that I’m not flexible. But the timeline is to do what we are trying to do now.’.

Asked if the job was proving to be tougher than he anticipated, Pocognoli said: ‘No. I think we nearly had a good game. It was just the score and the aspects in the boxes. That’s where there’s disappointment.

‘It’s step by step. And we have created a lot of chances in four of the six games. And in these six games we played one of them with 10 men and another where we were not on the level at all against Slovenia.’.

  • MK Dons will be targeting a seventh consecutive win in all competitions when they head to the One Call Stadium for Saturday’s League One encounter against Mansfield Town.
  • The visitors head into the weekend in ninth spot, while the Stags are two points worse off in 12th place in the League One table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 19 Nov 2026 22:55, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:00.

MK Dons will be targeting a seventh consecutive win in all competitions when they head to the One Call Stadium for Saturday’s League One encounter against Mansfield Town.

The visitors head into the weekend in ninth spot, while the Stags are two points worse off in 12th place in the League One table.

Mansfield occupy a midtable position after recording five wins, four draws and four defeats in 13 league games.

The Stags enjoyed a run of three wins in four league outings before they fell to a 2-0 home defeat against Notts County at the end of October.

Mansfield then played out a goalless draw against Wigan Athletic before they returned to winning ways with a 3-0 victory against sixth-tier Macclesfield in the FA Cup, setting up a second-round clash against fellow League Two side Colchester United.

Nigel Clough's charges netted three more goals in their EFL Trophy clash against Chesterfield, but they were left with nothing to show for their efforts after shipping four times in the final half-hour of a 5-3 defeat, ensuring they finished the group stage without a point to their name.

Mansfield will now turn their focus back to League One action, and they should fancy their chances of picking up at least a point, having lost just one of their six home games in the third tier this term (W3, D2).

Having failed to win their last three head-to-head home matches, Mansfield are aiming to beat MK Dons at the One Call Stadium for the first time since August 2006.

MK Dons, meanwhile, are in red-hot form after winning each of their last six competitive games, including four successive victories in League One.

After beating Stevenage, Bromley and Doncaster Rovers in the third tier, MK Dons kicked off their FA Cup campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over Swindon Town.

Paul Warne's charges backed up their FA Cup success with another 2-1 win in their EFL Trophy clash with Bromley, sending them through to the Round of 32 as Group H winners.

Sam Nombe then netted a brace in an emphatic 6-2 victory in last Saturday's home clash against Burton Albion, making it the third consecutive home league game in which MK Dons have scored four or more goals.

In stark contrast to their free-scoring home form, MK Dons have netted just seven goals across their six road trips in the third, although they only required one goal to claim their first away league win of the season against Stevenage last month.

Saturday's visitors can take confidence from the fact they have won two of their previous three away games against Mansfield, including a 2-1 success on their last visit to the One Call Stadium in March 2024.

Mansfield Town form (all competitions):.

MK Dons form (all competitions):.

Mansfield are expected to be without Liam Thompson, Lucas Akins and David McGoldrick due to injury.

Bailey Cargill, George Abbott and Louis Reed are making progress in their respective recoveries, but it remains to be seen whether they will be ready for Saturday’s fixture.

Mansfield will also assess the fitness of Deji Oshilaja and Frazer Blake-Tracey, the latter of whom picked up a hamstring glitch in the defeat to Chesterfield.

As for the visitors, Warne remains without the services of Ryan Barnett, Kane Wilson and Rushian Hepburn-Murphy.

Aaron Collins is back from international duty after making his Wales debut as a substitute in Tuesday’s 3-2 defeat to Portugal in the UEFA Nations League.

As League One’s top scorer with 13 goals, Collins is expected to lead the line alongside Nombe, which means Callum Paterson will likely have to settle for a place on the bench despite scoring in the last two competitive games.

Mansfield Town possible starting lineup:.

Roberts; Bowery, Blake-Tracy, Sweeney; Moriah-Welsh, Oates, Hendry, McLaughlin; Maris, Russell; Smith.

MK Dons possible starting lineup:.

Dennis; Ekpiteta, Sanders, Goode; Silvera, Gilbey, Wintle, Crowley, Campbell; Paterson, Nombe.

MK Dons will be full of confidence after winning six games on the bounce, and we think they will continue their impressive run of form against a Mansfield side that has won just one of their last four competitive outings.

Arteta’s players had come through some tricky assignments in winning their first seven matches of this season, but this was their toughest test yet and they failed it badly. They did not handle the emotions of the occasion particularly well, either: in stoppage time, a frustrated Declan Rice kicked out at Malick Yalcouyé. He was perhaps fortunate to avoid a red card.

These small things. If you win these small steps, and celebrate them as a win, then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 19 Nov 2026 22:55.

Coventry City welcome Crystal Palace to the Coventry Building Society Arena this weekend in a crucial Premier League relegation clash following the November international break.

Frank Lampard's 17th-placed Sky Blues sit just one point above the bottom three after a 3-1 defeat at Everton, though October home wins over Newcastle United and Sunderland offer encouragement as they chase consecutive top-flight victories on their own turf.

Meanwhile, fresh Palace boss Thomas Frank takes charge for the first time with less than a week of training under his belt, tasked with ending a four-match losing run and lifting the London club above their West Midlands hosts.

Here, Sports Mole takes a closer look at the head-to-head record and past meetings between Coventry and Crystal Palace.

Over 118 years have passed since Coventry City and Crystal Palace first locked horns - an FA Cup tie in January 1908 that ended in a 4-2 victory for the Eagles - and there have now been 114 competitive meetings between the two clubs across all competitions.

There is very little to separate the sides historically, with the Sky Blues holding the narrowest of edges on 41 victories, while Palace are hot on their heels with 38 wins and another 35 encounters have ended all square.

More than 14 years have elapsed since their most recent clash in March 2012, when the two teams shared the spoils in a 1-1 Championship draw in the West Midlands several months after Palace had edged a 2-1 victory at Selhurst Park.

Coventry's last triumphs in this fixture came during the 2010-11 campaign, when they recorded back-to-back 2-1 home wins in the FA Cup and Championship in January and February 2011 to avenge a 2-0 defeat in South London earlier that season.

Prior to that double, Palace had enjoyed a dominant spell over the Sky Blues, putting together a 10-match unbeaten run across all competitions between September 2005 and November 2009 that included seven wins and three draws.

That sequence featured five consecutive victories for the Londoners - highlighted by emphatic 4-1 and 4-2 away triumphs - before Coventry finally ended their hoodoo with a gritty 1-0 win at Selhurst Park in February 2010.

This weekend's showdown marks their first Premier League meeting in over 28 years, with the clubs last crossing paths in the top flight in February 1998 when Coventry ran out 3-0 winners in South London.

Across their six previous Premier League encounters, the Sky Blues hold the upper hand with two victories to Palace's one alongside three draws, and remarkably neither side has ever won a home game in the competition.

Palace's lone Premier League success in this fixture was a 4-1 away demolition in November 1994, whereas Coventry claimed 2-0 and 3-0 victories on the road in February 1995 and February 1998 respectively.

Before the Premier League era, Coventry were a formidable force against Palace in the old First Division, going unbeaten in their first 14 top-flight meetings between 1969 and 1990 - winning 10 and drawing four - before the Eagles finally broke their duck with a 2-1 win in December 1990.

Knockout meetings have been rare, with Palace winning three of their four cup ties - including 3-0 and 1-0 League Cup successes in 2002 and 2005 - while Coventry's most emphatic results in the fixture date back to their Division Three (South) days in the 1930s, when they dished out 8-0 and 8-1 home thrashings in 1932 and 1935.

I think this is the best Newcastle United team that is available now

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has not been an enjoyable season watching the Newcastle United team so far and that’s being nice about, it may be hyperbolic to say we’ve been as bad as some of what we saw under the dark days of Mike Ashley, but the cluelessness of our play at times this year has definitely brought up memories of John Carver and Steve Bruce for me.
  • For the record, I think persisting with a manager who is making Ruben Amorim seem flexible isn’t a great idea, but trying to think of how with the current squad we might be able to make the best of the situation.
  • Recent findings suggest that let us start with the issues for Matthias Jaissle’ s preferred system, firstly at the back where being honest I think our back five who started against Fulham are ok together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has not been an enjoyable season watching the Newcastle United team so far and that’s being nice about, it may be hyperbolic to say we’ve been as bad as some of what we saw under the dark days of Mike Ashley, but the cluelessness of our play at times this year has definitely brought up memories of John Carver and Steve Bruce for me.

For the record, I think persisting with a manager who is making Ruben Amorim seem flexible isn’t a great idea, but trying to think of how with the current squad we might be able to make the best of the situation.

Recent findings suggest that let us start with the issues for Matthias Jaissle’ s preferred system, firstly at the back where being honest I think our back five who started against Fulham are ok together. Hornicek has made a few mistakes but overall, he’s made some good saves, and his ball playing is a big help.

At LB Lewis Hall is an absolute Unicorn and could play in any system, at RB Dedic is a bit defensively suspect but has a lot of energy and gets up and down the line. CB is where the theoretical concern is, Jaissles system requires pacy ball playing CBs, who are good when left 1v1 and the only one of ours who fits that bill in some way is Thiaw, who is generally great but has the odd Titus moment.

It has been revealed that our other CBs just aren’t fits in this system, none have the pace, Schar is fading a bit even on the ball and Botman has never been the same since our medical staff got their hands on him. I’m not that worried about this area of the pitch too much though as despite Dan Burn being slow and not the greatest on the ball he won’t overplay, and he will put his body on the line and win as much as he can. I think there is always a place for an old school CB. So, keep that back five from the Fulham game together and we should be ok there.

Now moving into midfield and we need two for the double pivot, Joelinton gives you physically but he doesn’t have the guile or composure required to play there week in and week out (though what I’d give to have him vs Arsenal on Saturday). Ramsey is pretty anonymous there, Willock despite once every few years looking like he could be a great destroyer (Hull this season and the first half vs Forest (4-3) a couple of years ago) is way too inconsistent and finally Bamba who looks lost in his limited minutes and has hardly had a look in.

As such, it comes down for me to two of three, we have Nico who’s shown his quality in a couple of games (Palace/Spurs) but has ran around and fouled a lot in others, Miley who can look like a world beater but then also get overran and finally Steur who’s great on the ball but has defensive limitations at this point in his development. All three lack legs but from what we have they are definitely our best options.

According to recent reports, I think when thinking of who is best in the double pivot we need to think of who is going to be in the 10 with them. So far this year it has been Wissa and Willock there the most with the odd moment of Ramsey.

Wissa after one good game against Liverpool looks like he’s put his jeans back on and just isn’t suitable, Willock has his moments but like in the pivot he’s incredibly inconsistent and can coast for larger parts of the game and finally Ramsey while not seeming like an awful player has so little impact. I think going for him rather than El Khannouss will be one that bites us far years.

In a recent development, so, not an inspiring group of options in that 10 role which is key to this system working, we need someone dropping between the lines, who can then turn and make quick accurate passes to our front line. None of the three mentioned can do that at any sort of decent level and it kills our attacking play. I do think we have one player who could thrive here.

Recent findings suggest that that player is Sean Steur whose passing range is probably the best we have and his footballing brain belies his years. You may think it’s not his position. he plays deeper and he’s very good there, and to that I say we need to look to the south coast and to Brighton and one of this season’s best players in Pascal Gross.

You see Gross often lines up as the 10 for Brighton and his passing ability and nous causes chaos but he doesn’t just stay at the top end of the field, he has freedom to wander and drop deep and start attacks. I can see Steur not only being able to do this but be able to thrive in this role. The added bonus is as we have two other midfielders behind him his defensive limitations are covered.

Because of this, in the middle of the pitch I’d want to see Steur in the 10 and Miley and Nico in the double pivot, there is a risk of not having a runner in there but you’d hope with the technical ability of those three we can exert a degree of control on games and set a firmer base in front of the defence.

We then move to the wingers, where in Jaissle’s systems the wingers need to be comfortable coming inside and creating space for the full-backs to overlap leading to overloads of the opposition defence. One of our massive problems is on the right-hand side we have two wingers who being polite are touchline wingers and being more blunt, Jacob Murphy puts in the occasional good ball but his all-round game is chronic and Elanga reminds me of Obertan and not because of the pace (I’m waiting for him to forget to take the ball with him when he’s running through at some point).

Recent findings suggest that on the left Barnes always puts up a good stat line but his unwillingness to have a go at full-backs combined with his low success rate of beating his man puts us on the back foot a lot. The one thing Barnes does well is he makes a lot of runs, maybe with someone in that ten who can find him he would offer more.

Toure is so raw if he were a steak a Frenchman would send him back to cook some more, he has moments, but you just don’t know what you would get with him. I’d be tempted to play him more purely because he is one of our only options who will get at his full-back and I think he may actually be better playing on the right in the long run.

The last player to throw into the mix is Pardo, the lad wants to be a striker but that is very optimistic, and I think it’s clear he’s a winger and that’s where he needs to play most likely on the left. So again, on the wings not an inspiring bunch, I’d like to see Pardo getting game time on the left and it’s between Toure or Barnes for the right (Murphy and Elanga only look good when the other is playing). I think it would have to be Toure as we need to see what he can do, he’s a left footer so would cut inside more naturally, and he can make something happen.

Sources indicate that the last position is probably the most worrying because at previous clubs Matthias Jaissle has used strikers like Toney and Sesko as his focal points, physical centre forwards who can put pressure on the opposition centre backs and hold the ball up. As mentioned before, Wissa often looks like he is playing in Jeans and even when he gets on the ball, he has been less than inspiring and doesn’t have the physicality to hold the ball up or the quality to link the play up. Our other option is Osula who can be chaotic and has moments where you think there might be a player there but then he does things like not run in a straight line when chasing a pass or get shrugged off the ball despite his physical gifts. There’s something there but he has a very headless vibe. At this point he’s clearly the better option but if Wilson gets his act together and does something in January a CF is a must.

So, for now a 4-2-3-1 Newcastle United team of:.

Hornicek, Dedic, Thiaw, Burn, Hall, Nico, Miley, Toure, Steur, Pardo, Osula.

This is what I think is the best we’ve got and I’d like to see this line up at some point soon, but I think the key thing we need to try is moving Steur into the free/10 role, to let him try and solve our creativity issues.

Anyway, back to reality and Saturday coming, fingers crossed for the oncoming onslaught of the Opulent Stoke. Fingers crossed and Howay the Mags.

How have these first few months at Milan been? Are you raising your game?

How is your relationship with Amorim?

“He talks to me about what to do with the ball and to do my best.”.

Why this difference in performance between Serie A and the Europa League?

“It’s hard to say… There have been games where we haven’t performed well due to silly mistakes, but I think we need to push forward from now on and get back on track for the Europa League. We have the right team to do it. We need to win and be at our best in every game.”.

What has struck you most about the fans in Italy these past months?

Do you think Milan can win the Scudetto?
